The defendant Nos.1-2, 12-17, 18-21 and 22-23 contested the suit by filing separate written statements contending that their predecessor-in-interest took the settlement of the suit land from the landlords and had been possessing the same and, thereafter, through successive transfers the contesting defendants have become the owners of the suit land and that the impugned kabala is the genuine one. 

 8. The case of the government is that the suit land originally belonged to Sarada Prossad Roy Chowdhury, Amulya Prosad Roy Chowdhury, Aboni Prosad Roy Chawdhury, Atul Prosan Roy Chowdhury, Amiya Prosad Roy Chowdhury and Arun Prosad Roy Chowdhury. S.S record of-right was prepared in their names. The defendants in their written statements also admitted that the suit originally belonged to aforesaid Sarada Prosad Roy Chowdhury and others. The further case of the government was that the suit land was vested in the government-as per provision of Section 3 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On the other hand, the defendants claimed that aforesaid Sarada Prosad Roy Chowdhury and others settled the suit land to their predecessor-in-interest. S.A. record of right Kas prepared in their names. Now, the first question is as to whether the government had acquired the land as per provision of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or not.

 "25. Sub-section 1 of section 39 laid down that compensation payable to a rent receiver, a cultivating raiyat, a cultivating under-raiyat or a non-agricultural tenant, in respect of the acquisition of lands in his khash possession which he is not entitled to retain under section 20, shall be determined in accordance with the table mentioned in section 39. Sub-section 2 of section 39 then states that said that any dispute regarding classification of the lands for the purpose of sub-section 1 shall be referred to the prescribed revenue authority whose decision there-on shall be final. Section 40 deals with preliminary publication of Compensation Assessment-roll and then section 41 deals with appeal which can be presented with regard to assessment of compensation against the decision of the revenue authority. It is after all these that under section 42 the final publication of Compensation Assessment-roll is made. Section 44 then says that on the publication of a notification in the official gazette under subsection 2 of section 43 declaring that compensation mentioned in that section shall ensue, one of them, being that all the interests that are acquirable under the Act but have not acquired under Chapter-II of the Act shall "with the effect from the first day of the agricultural year nest following the date of publication of such notification in the official Gazettee, be deemed to have been acquired by the Government and vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances". 

 26, A close reading of the provisions made in the sections 42, 43 and 44 of the Act point to inevitable conclusions that every interest which is liable to be acquired under the Act has to be paid for and that except in the cases of acquisition under Chapter-II of the Act the interests which are acquirable vest in the Government only if assessment of compensation in regard to the same has been made and-published as provided in the Act."

They could not produce any documentary evidence to substantiate their claim of settlement. In addition, there is no proof apparent on the face of the record that the government had not followed the pre-scribed procedure under sections 3, 42 or 43 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.
